metaDescription: Five cordless electric snow shovels compared on clearing width, battery platform, throw distance and weight for decks, steps and short driveways.
expertTake: The EGO SNS1201 is the best overall pick for owners already on a 56V platform, and the Snow Joe 24V kit is the value pick for light snow on decks and steps. Anyone with a long driveway or deep, wet snow should skip this category and buy a proper single-stage blower.
introParagraphs: An electric snow shovel is a small auger in a lightweight body, pushed ahead of you like a vacuum. It scoops and throws a narrow strip of snow, which makes it a deck, step and walkway tool rather than a driveway machine.

The category is crowded with near-identical imports, so the useful differences come down to battery capacity, clearing depth, weight and whether the maker will still sell packs in three winters. This guide sorts those out and says plainly where the tool runs out of ability.

products.name: EGO Power+ SNS1201 12-Inch Cordless Snow Shovel Kit
products.description:
The EGO SNS1201 pairs a 12 inch auger housing with a 56V battery from a platform that covers mowers, trimmers and blowers. A directional dial adjusts the throw across about 60 degrees, so you can aim snow off a step without turning the whole machine. The kit includes the 2.5Ah pack and a fast charger, which is enough to start without extra purchases.

The tradeoff is width and pack size. At 12 inches it clears a narrower strip than the 16 inch VOLTASK 48V, and a 2.5Ah pack holds less energy than the 4Ah packs bundled with cheaper rivals. If you own other EGO tools, the real advantage is that spare packs you already have double your runtime. Buyers of imports should also ask whether the pack is sold separately, because a tool whose proprietary battery is discontinued becomes scrap the first time the original pack fades, usually after two or three winters of regular charging.

Ownership is easy because a known brand keeps replacement batteries and parts available for years. Store the pack indoors, since cold sharply reduces lithium output, and clear the auger with the battery removed after any jam.
products.bestFor: Owners already on the EGO 56V platform who want a deck and step tool.
pros: Part of a large 56V battery platform
Charger and battery included in the kit
Established brand with long parts support
cons: Narrower than the 13 to 17 inch rivals

products.name: 24V Snow Joe 13-Inch Cordless Snow Shovel Kit 4.0Ah
products.description:
Snow Joe has sold electric snow shovels longer than most of the imports, and this 24V kit shows it. A 400W motor drives a 13 inch auger and the 4.0Ah pack is claimed to move about 1,620 pounds of snow per charge. The kit also adds a protective cover and an ice scraper, small items that matter when you store the tool in a cold garage.

The cost is power. A 400W motor is modest next to the 1200W brushless units in this group, so it slows in packed or wet snow. Against the EGO 12 inch it gives a slightly wider path and a bigger battery, but without a platform behind it.

Easy ownership is the draw: a long-established seller, a straightforward tool and a battery that charges in a few hours. Keep the auger clear of ice and do not push it into gravel. Because the kit ships with a cover, use it: a bare tool left in an unheated shed collects frost in the chute, and stored dry it will be ready after the first overnight storm of the year without any fuss.
products.bestFor: Light snowfall on decks, steps and short paved paths.
pros: Wider 13 inch path than the EGO
Cover and scraper in the kit
cons: No battery platform for other tools
Claimed capacity is a manufacturer figure

products.name: VOLTASK 24V 13-Inch Cordless Snow Shovel 4Ah 9.3 lb
products.description:
The VOLTASK 24V is built around low weight. At about 9.3 pounds it is the lightest machine in this group, which matters because you hold it at arm's length across a whole deck. A directional plate lets you choose where the snow lands instead of fighting the throw.

The tradeoff is power and depth. It shares the 13 inch width of the Snow Joe, but with less established backing and a smaller motor than the brushless 48V VOLTASK. For a few inches of powder on steps it works; deeper or heavier snow will stall it.

Ownership is simple. Keep the battery indoors, brush off the auger after use and avoid slush, which freezes inside the housing and ices the blades.
products.bestFor: Buyers who need the lightest tool for steps and decks.
cons: Newer brand with less parts support

products.name: VOLTASK 48V 16-Inch Electric Snow Shovel With Wheels 1200W
products.description:
This VOLTASK steps up to a 16 inch path, an 8 inch depth and a 1200W brushless motor spinning the auger at about 2000 RPM. Wheels take the weight off your arms and make it feel like a small blower rather than a shovel. For a sidewalk and a short drive, that extra width means fewer passes.

The tradeoff is weight and cost. Wheels and a bigger battery add mass, so it is no longer the tool you carry up steps, and it has less of a track record than EGO or Snow Joe. Against the MZK 40V 17 inch, it is a little narrower but the wheels make it easier to push.

Brushless motors need no brush replacement, and the main upkeep is the auger. Wipe it dry after every session, because meltwater trapped between the auger and the housing refreezes overnight and can stall the motor on the next start, which owners often mistake for a dead battery. Keep it off gravel and let the pack warm before charging after a freezing night.
products.bestFor: Sidewalks and short driveways where width matters more than carry weight.

products.name: MZK 40V 17-Inch Brushless Electric Snow Shovel Two Batteries
products.description:
The MZK is the widest and most powerful machine here, with a 17 inch path, a brushless motor claimed at 2000W and two 4.0Ah packs in the box. The maker claims up to 40 minutes of running and an area of about 1,500 square feet per charge pair. Two batteries is the real value, because one charges while the other works.

The tradeoff is that it behaves like a small single-stage blower in a shovel body, and it is the heaviest of the group. Compared with the 16 inch wheeled VOLTASK, it clears a stripe an inch wider but gives up wheels.

Because it moves the most snow per minute, it also asks the most of its packs, so rotate them rather than draining one to empty every time. Plan on storing packs indoors, checking auger clearance often and keeping spare shear hardware if the manual lists any. Treat the claimed throw as a best case in light snow. With two packs the practical routine is to start on one, swap when the machine slows, and put the spent pack on the charger indoors, so a long walk and a short drive can be finished in one outing instead of two.
products.bestFor: Homeowners with a long walk and a small drive who want two batteries in the box.
pros: Widest path in the group at 17 inches
Brushless motor with high auger speed

buyingCriteria.explanation: Width sets how many passes a path takes, and depth sets how much snow the auger can swallow before it stalls. The EGO at 12 inches and the MZK at 17 inches sit at opposite ends, and the VOLTASK 48V adds an 8 inch depth rating. A wider unit saves time on a long walk but weighs more, so match width to the length of the path, not to the biggest number on the box. Also measure the narrowest point you must clear, such as a gate or a porch gap, because a 17 inch body that cannot fit through it is worse than a 12 inch one that can.

Voltage alone says little; what matters is volts times amp-hours, so the Snow Joe 24V at 4.0Ah holds roughly 96 watt-hours while the EGO 56V at 2.5Ah holds about 140. Dual 4.0Ah packs on the MZK give the longest working time. If you already own tools on a platform such as EGO, spare packs you own are the cheapest runtime.

Brushless motors such as those in the VOLTASK 48V and MZK run cooler and last longer than brushed ones. The Snow Joe uses a 400W motor, which is enough for powder but slows in packed snow. A common mistake is trusting a peak wattage claim; look for continuous power and for how much snow the machine can handle in a real pass.

The VOLTASK 24V weighs about 9.3 pounds and the wheeled VOLTASK 48V weighs noticeably more, which changes how the tool feels after ten minutes. Lighter units suit steps and decks where you lift the tool. Wheels suit flat walks where you push it. Pick the weight that fits where you will actually use it. If anyone with a bad shoulder or wrist will run the tool, favour the lightest body or the wheeled unit, since fatigue shows up as sloppy passes and missed ice patches long before it shows up as pain.

A directional dial like the EGO's 60 degree control or a plate like the VOLTASK's decides whether snow lands on the lawn or back on the path. Without it you shovel the same snow twice. Check that the control can be set with a glove on and that it holds its position under vibration. Throwing into the wind returns a surprising share of the snow to your own boots, so a control that lets you change direction quickly is more useful than a long maximum throw distance on paper.

Lithium packs lose output near 0 degrees F, so store them indoors and fit them just before use. Wet heavy snow also drains packs faster and stalls small motors, which is why the 400W Snow Joe suits powder more than slush. If your region gets heavy, wet falls, step up to the brushless units or a full blower. A useful habit is to clear snow early and often in two shallow passes rather than waiting for the storm to finish, because a few inches of fresh powder is within these tools' ability while a foot of compacted slush is not.

specDecoder.meaning: The width of the strip the auger clears in a single pass. Wider means fewer passes but more weight.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EGO is 12 inches while the MZK is 17 inches.

specDecoder.meaning: Voltage times amp-hours gives watt-hours, the real energy store. Compare that figure rather than voltage alone.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Snow Joe 24V 4.0Ah and EGO 56V 2.5Ah differ in stored energy.

specDecoder.meaning: A motor without carbon brushes that runs cooler and lasts longer. It usually delivers more torque per watt.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MZK and the 48V VOLTASK are brushless while the Snow Joe is a 400W unit.

specDecoder.meaning: How far the machine throws light snow, measured by the maker in ideal conditions.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MZK claims 30 feet and the EGO 25 feet, and wet snow shortens both.

howWeEvaluated.title: Clearing capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared clearing width and depth from the listings. The EGO at 12 inches and the MZK at 17 inches define the range. Depth ratings were considered only where the maker published them.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery energy
howWeEvaluated.description: We multiplied voltage by amp-hours to compare stored energy. Dual-pack kits like the MZK scored higher on runtime than single-pack kits. Platform support counted for the EGO.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor design
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered brushless versus brushed motors and the claimed power. The Snow Joe at 400W and the VOLTASK at 1200W show the spread. Claims are treated as claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared body weight, wheels and grip design. The VOLTASK 24V at 9.3 pounds sets the light end. Heavier units scored lower on steps, and a lighter body was credited only when the motor and pack still looked adequate for the stated depth.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed brand history, parts support and storage needs from the listings and owner feedback patterns. Established sellers like Snow Joe and EGO scored better on long-term support.

cards.label: Shovel style
cards.text: The VOLTASK 24V, Snow Joe and EGO are carried and steered by hand. They are light and fit steps, decks and tight corners, but they tire your arms on long runs.

cards.label: Wheeled style
cards.text: The VOLTASK 48V wheeled unit and the MZK behave like small blowers, with the machine's weight on the ground. They cover walks faster but are harder to carry up stairs.

howToChoose.note: Choose shovel style for steps and decks, wheeled for long, flat walks.

rows: Want two packs in the box

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for low weight, a directional discharge and a narrow body that can turn on a step. Wide wheeled machines are awkward on small landings.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The VOLTASK 24V at 9.3 pounds and the EGO SNS1201 with its 60 degree dial fit this job best. The Snow Joe 24V is a close third.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if your path is long, where the MZK 40V or the VOLTASK 48V cut the number of passes. Also spend more for the EGO if you will use its battery in other tools.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you only clear steps and a small deck. The Snow Joe kit or the VOLTASK 24V is plenty.

maintenance.why: Cold cuts lithium output. Fit the pack just before clearing.
Wet snow freezes in the housing and stalls the auger on the next start.
A stuck auger can start suddenly. Remove the battery first.
Storing a full or empty pack shortens its life.
Worn rubber and plastic tips lose throw distance and clear less.

faq.q: Can an electric snow shovel handle a driveway?
faq.a: A short paved drive in light snow, yes, but a long drive or deep snow, no. These tools clear a narrow strip with small motors. For a standard driveway, a single-stage blower is the better tool.

Most clear about 6 to 8 inches of light snow in a pass according to the makers. Wet snow reduces that sharply. Take shallower passes in heavy conditions, working from the top of the layer down, so the auger never has to swallow the full depth at once and the battery is not asked for its peak current on every stroke.
For anything beyond steps and a deck, yes. The MZK includes two for that reason. With one pack, plan on a charge break midway.
Higher voltage generally means a more powerful brushless system, as in the VOLTASK 48V, but the pack and motor design matter more. Compare watt-hours and continuous power, not the number alone.

faq.q: Can I use one on gravel?
faq.a: No. Gravel is thrown by the auger and damages plastic parts. Use it only on paved or solid surfaces.

faq.q: How do I keep the battery working in the cold?
faq.a: Store it indoors and insert it just before use. A cold pack delivers less power and trips protection earlier. Do not charge a frozen pack.
